headline: When Smart Gadgets Stop Being Smart: The Rise of the 'Smart Home Graveyard'

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: Some kitchen ovens, doorbells, and other home gadgets are called 'smart' because they connect to the internet and an app on your phone. A company called June made a very fancy smart oven that could look at food with a camera and cook it perfectly. But then a bigger company bought June and later turned off the special internet service that made the oven smart. Now the oven still bakes food, but it can't use the app, get updates, or use its camera anymore. This has happened to many other smart gadgets too, like smart doorbells, robot vacuums, and smart light bulbs. Companies sometimes stop paying for the servers that make these gadgets smart, because it costs money to keep them running. When that happens, the gadgets still work in a basic way, but they lose their coolest features. People who study technology say companies should build gadgets that still work well even without the internet, using buttons or other simple controls. That way, if a company shuts down its servers, your gadget won't become almost useless. This matters because families spend a lot of money on these smart gadgets, expecting them to work for years.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Ten years ago, a company created a very fancy smart oven called the June Oven. It had a camera and used artificial intelligence to recognize food, like a chicken breast, and cook it perfectly. It cost a lot of money, but people loved it. Later, a company called Weber bought June and eventually decided to shut down the online service that made the oven 'smart.' Without that service, the oven still bakes food, but it lost its app, camera features, and any future updates. This didn't just happen to June. Many other smart home gadgets—like certain robot vacuums, smart light bulbs, security systems, and speakers—have also lost their smart features over the past couple of years. Usually, a big company buys a smaller company that made a cool gadget, and then decides it isn't profitable enough to keep supporting. Keeping servers running costs money, so when a company stops seeing enough profit, it often just turns off the service. Sometimes gadgets get rescued by fans who find ways to make them work using local, offline systems instead of the internet. But most gadgets, like June's oven, are stuck as a 'smart' device without any smartness left. Experts believe there are ways to prevent this problem. Companies could build gadgets with buttons and offline features from the very beginning, so the device still works well even if the online service disappears someday. They also suggest that shoppers look for gadgets that can work without needing the internet at all. This story is important because people are spending a lot of money on gadgets that might stop working the way they were promised, sometimes after just a few years.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: A decade ago, some former Apple engineers built an incredibly advanced smart oven called the June Oven. It had a built-in scale, a camera, and artificial intelligence that could recognize different foods and cook them perfectly. Even though it was expensive, it built a loyal following. Eventually, the company was bought by Weber, the grill company, which stopped making the ovens and recently shut down the app and cloud service that powered its 'smart' features. Now the oven can still bake and roast food, but none of its intelligent features work anymore, and it can't be updated or repaired with new parts. This is part of a much bigger pattern. Many once-popular smart home gadgets—like certain robot vacuums, security systems, light bulbs, and buttons—have lost their smart features after the companies behind them were bought out or simply decided it wasn't profitable to keep running the necessary servers. This happens because 'smart' features usually rely on cloud servers, which cost money to maintain. When a company no longer profits from a product, continuing to pay for that upkeep often doesn't make financial sense to them, even though customers are left with gadgets that don't work as promised. Sometimes there are happy endings. A few devices have been 'rescued' by loyal fans or by companies that release their software as free, open-source code so others can keep supporting it. For example, Bose did this with one of its speaker systems, and a smartwatch company called Pebble was revived by its original founder after fans kept it alive using an alternative service. But these rescues are rare exceptions, not the rule. Technology experts and consumer advocates argue that this is a warning sign of a larger problem in how 'smart' devices are designed. They're pushing for laws that would require companies to let devices keep some basic functions—like local, offline control—even after the company shuts down its official app or servers. They also encourage manufacturers to design products that don't completely depend on the cloud in the first place, using physical buttons and offline communication methods. For anyone shopping for smart home gadgets, the takeaway is to look for products that can still function without an internet connection, since cloud-only features can vanish at any time, no matter how much money you spent.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: In 2013, a startup founded by ex-Apple engineers introduced the June Oven, an ambitious countertop appliance equipped with a built-in scale, a camera, and artificial intelligence capable of identifying foods and cooking them precisely. Despite a steep price tag, it developed a devoted fan base. But last week, June's smart features died for good. Weber, the grill manufacturer that acquired June in 2021 and had already stopped manufacturing the ovens in 2022, shut down the app and cloud servers that powered its intelligent functions. The oven can still bake and roast, but its camera-based food recognition, remote app control, and software updates are permanently gone—and if the device is ever factory reset, it may become unusable altogether. This isn't an isolated case. Over the last two years alone, numerous smart home products—including security systems, thermostats, robot vacuums, smart plugs, speakers, and light bulbs—have suffered similar fates as their parent companies shut down supporting cloud services. The pattern tends to follow a familiar arc: a small, innovative company builds an impressive connected gadget, attracts users, and is eventually acquired by a larger corporation. That corporation, often more focused on quarterly profits than nurturing a niche product, eventually decides the ongoing cost of running cloud servers outweighs the revenue the product generates, and shuts the service down. Because many 'smart' features depend entirely on manufacturer-controlled servers rather than working through local, offline connections, once those servers go dark, so does much of the product's usefulness. Occasionally, devices get a second life. Passionate user communities have found creative ways to link certain 'orphaned' gadgets to Home Assistant, a free, open-source smart home platform that doesn't rely on any single company's servers. In rare instances, companies have even open-sourced their software, allowing outside developers to keep a product's features alive independently, as Bose did with one of its speaker lines. But such rescues remain the exception rather than the rule; most abandoned gadgets, like June's oven, are left in a permanently diminished state. This trend has prompted growing calls for reform. Consumer advocacy groups are pushing for legislation requiring manufacturers to enable local control options before shutting down cloud services, so devices remain functional even after a company's support ends. Technology commentators argue that manufacturers should adopt a 'design for death' philosophy from the very beginning—building products with physical controls and local wireless protocols like Zigbee, Z-Wave, Thread, or Bluetooth, so that core functions survive independent of any corporate server. Some companies have already softened the blow by offering refunds or free replacement devices when discontinuing a product line. For consumers, this story underscores an important lesson: any smart device relying entirely on a company's cloud service is only as durable as that company's business decisions.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: A decade ago, a team of former Apple engineers unveiled the June Oven, a $1,495 smart countertop appliance featuring a built-in scale, restaurant-grade heating elements, an internal camera, and machine-learning software capable of identifying specific foods and cooking them with precision. It became a beloved, if niche, product among early adopters of connected home technology. Last week, however, June's intelligent features were permanently deactivated. Weber, the grill manufacturer that acquired June in January 2021 and discontinued production of the ovens in 2022, shut down the app and cloud infrastructure underpinning the device's smart capabilities. The oven will continue to function as a conventional toaster oven, but its camera-based recognition system, remote app controls, and software updates are gone for good, with no replacement parts or technical support available going forward. Weber reportedly considered open-sourcing June's technology to let outside developers keep it alive but ultimately declined, citing intellectual property entanglements with its own proprietary smart home platform. June's fate is emblematic of a much larger and accelerating trend often described as the 'smart home graveyard.' In just the past two years, a long list of once-prominent connected products—including Nest Secure security systems, early Nest thermostats, Belkin's WeMo devices, Neato robot vacuums, the Brava smart oven, Logitech's Pop buttons, Bose's SoundTouch speakers, and Sengled's smart bulbs—have lost some or all of their cloud-dependent functionality after their manufacturers discontinued supporting servers. The underlying business dynamics tend to follow a recognizable pattern: an innovative startup builds a compelling connected device, is later acquired by a larger corporation, and eventually has its product deprioritized once ongoing server costs no longer align with corporate profit expectations. Because many smart features rely exclusively on manufacturer-hosted cloud servers rather than local, offline protocols, discontinuing that infrastructure can instantly strip a device of most of its advertised value, even though the physical hardware still technically works. Occasionally, dedicated user communities manage informal rescues by connecting orphaned devices to Home Assistant, an open-source, locally controlled smart home platform that operates independently of any single manufacturer's servers. In rarer cases, companies proactively open-source their software, as Bose did with its SoundTouch platform, allowing continued community-led support after official discontinuation. Consumer advocacy organizations, including Consumer Reports, are now lobbying for legislation that would require manufacturers to enable local control options before shutting down cloud services entirely, ensuring products retain baseline functionality independent of corporate decision-making. Industry commentators argue for a 'design for death' philosophy, urging companies to build in physical controls and interoperable local wireless protocols—such as Zigbee, Z-Wave, Thread, and Bluetooth—so that essential functions persist regardless of a manufacturer's future business fortunes. Some companies have softened these transitions through refunds or free replacement hardware, though experts note such gestures don't fully compensate for lost functionality. Ultimately, this story raises fundamental questions about durability, ownership, and trust in an era where a product's usefulness can depend as much on a company's balance sheet as on its physical engineering.

questions: If you owned a smart gadget that suddenly lost its 'smart' features, how would that change the way you trust technology companies in the future?
Why do you think companies sometimes stop supporting gadgets even when people are still using and loving them, and is that fair to customers?

What responsibilities do you think companies should have to customers when they decide to discontinue a smart product, and how could schools or communities encourage more responsible technology design?
